questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in counterclockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C={C}_{1}\cup \{-{C}_{2}\}\cup {C}_{3},

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/c0a4f042748ddadd824bed4ee71bca9724d7ca7dcc376a0ccf7c1353d59ec4fc.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(-2,2)$ to the point $B(-1,2),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $B(-1,2)$ to the point $D(-1,0).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-\frac{7}{2},$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x-y)\,i+(y-x)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the vertical line segment from $B$ to $D.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =b+t(d-b) \\  & =⟨-1,2⟩+t(⟨-1,0⟩-⟨-1,2⟩) \\  & =⟨-1,2-2t⟩ \\  & =-\,i+(2-2t)\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=-1$ and $y=2-2t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(x-y)\,i+(y-x)\,j \\  & =(-1-(2-2t))\,i+(2-2t-(-1))\,j \\  & =(-3+2t)\,i+(3-2t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-2t)j \\  & =-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =((-3+2t)\,i+(3-2t)\,j)\cdot (-2\,j) \\  & =(3-2t)\cdot (-2) \\  & =4t-6\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-\frac{7}{2}+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{2}+{\int }_{0}^{1}(4t-6)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{7}{2}+[2{t}^{2}-6t]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{7}{2}+[2({1}^{2})-6(1)-0] \\  & =-\frac{7}{2}-4 \\  & =-\frac{15}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a the line segment from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $B(0,1),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of the line segment from the point $B(0,1)$ to the point $D(1,1).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r=-\frac{3}{2},$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x-2y)\,i+(y-x)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the second integral, so we only need to work out the first.

The path ${C}_{1}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$  It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =⟨-2,0⟩+t(⟨0,1⟩-⟨-2,0⟩) \\  & =⟨-2+2t,t⟩ \\  & =(-2+2t)i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=-2+2t$ and $y=t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =(x-2y)\,i+(y-x)\,j \\  & =((-2+2t)-2t)\,i+(t-(-2+2t))\,j \\  & =-2\,i+(2-t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2+2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =2\,i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =(-2\,i+(2-t)\,j)\cdot (2\,i+j) \\  & =-2-t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t+(-\frac{3}{2}) \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-2-t)\,\text{d}t-\frac{3}{2} \\  & ={[-2t-\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{1}-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =[-2(1)-\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}-0]-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<2.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y={t}^{2}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t)) & =x\,i+y\,j \\  & =t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})j \\  & =i+2t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j)\cdot (i+2t\,j) \\  & =t+2{t}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}F({r}_{1}(t))\cdot {r}_{1}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t-2 \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(t+2{t}^{3})\,\text{d}t-2 \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2}-2 \\  & =[2+8]-2 \\  & =10-2 \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/0e4a78829ce8d1135d46dda1db59c968c0306937d9c5a45b24fa41648a679ea4.png)

The path ${C}_{1}$ consists of a line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $A(2,0),$ and the path ${C}_{2}$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(2,0)$ to the point $B(1,1).$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2,$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=(x+y)\,i+(x-y)\,j,$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path ${C}_{2}$ is the line segment from $A$ to $B.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =a+t(b-a) \\  & =⟨2,0⟩+t(⟨1,1⟩-⟨2,0⟩) \\  & =⟨2-t,t⟩ \\  & =(2-t)\,i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<1.$ Along this segment, we have $x=2-t$ and $y=t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(x+y)\,i+(x-y)\,j \\  & =(2-t+t)\,i+(2-t-t)\,j \\  & =2\,i+(2-2t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =-i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =(2\,i+(2-2t)\,j)\cdot (-i+j) \\  & =-2+(2-2t) \\  & =-2t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2+{\int }_{0}^{1}(-2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2-{t}^{2}{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =2-(1-0) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Given that ${\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r=2,$ evaluate ${\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r,$ where $F(x,y)=x\,i$ and $C={C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

Let ${C}_{2}$ be the section of parabola $y=4-{x}^{2}$ from $A$ to $B.$ Then,
 $-{C}_{2}$ will be the same path but travelled from $B$ to $A.$ The path $-{C}_{2}$ can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t)=t\,i+(4-{t}^{2})\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<t<2.$ Along this curve, we have $x=t$ and $y=4-{t}^{2}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =x\,i=t\,i.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4-{t}^{2})j \\  & =i-2t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =(t\,i)\cdot (i-2t\,j) \\  & =t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =2-{\int }_{0}^{2}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2-{\int }_{0}^{2}t\,\text{d}t \\  & =2-{[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2-[\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}] \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Establishing the Connection With Line Integrals of Scalar Fields
canonical_examples.problem: Let $\mathbf{F}(x,y) = (3x+2) \: \mathbf{i} - y^3 \: \mathbf{j}$ and let $C$ be a path in $\mathbb R^2.$ Write $\displaystyle \int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r}$ in the form $\displaystyle\int_C P(x,y)\,\textrm d x +  Q(x,y)\,\textrm d y.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a piecewise-smooth path $C$ and a vector field 

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y) = P(x,y) \: \mathbf{i} + Q(x,y) \: \mathbf{j}
$$

defined on $C,$ we have

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf{F} \cdot \text{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_C P(x,y) \: \text{d}x + Q(x,y) \: \text{d}y.
$$

In our case, $P = 3x+2$ and $Q = -y^3.$ Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{C}(3x+2)\,\text{d}x-{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Establishing the Connection With Line Integrals of Scalar Fields

Example: 
                    Using the Properties of Line Integrals of Vector-Valued Functions
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/38ab4af726729b5c9804f4aa13801d637e5e62eda085d6611174586827ef8c11.png)

Consider the integral $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $C$ is the closed polygonal path $FGHF$ shown above, traversed in the **clockwise** direction. Express this integral as a sum of line integrals along $C_1, C_2,$ and $C_3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can represent $C,$ which is traversed in clockwise, as the union of $3$ paths:

$$
C = \{-C_1\} \cup \{-C_2\} \cup C_3,
$$

where $-C_1$ and $-C_2$ are the same paths as $C_1$ and $C_2$ but traversed in the opposite direction.

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{-{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{-{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r-{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot \text{d}r.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating the Line Integral of a Vector-Valued Function Along a Union of Curves
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/001487e4a94988a24d15702a18692e9deb2495a7cc7ec5c9f71b98fea13e0ce8.png)

The path $C_1$ consists of a line segment from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $O(0,0),$ and the path $C_2$ consists of a line segment from the point $O(0,0)$ to the point $B(1,1).$

Given that $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = -4,$ evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r},$ where $\mathbf{F}(x, y) = (2x-3y) \,\mathbf{i} + (2y-5x)\,\mathbf {j}$ and $C = C_1\cup C_2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the fact that

$$
\int\limits_{C} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r} = \int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}
+
 \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{r}.
$$

We're given the value of the first integral, so we only need to work out the second.

The path $C_2$ is the line segment from $O$ to $B.$ It can be parametrized as

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}(t) & =b+t(c-b) \\  & =⟨0,0⟩+t(⟨1,1⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\  & =⟨t,t⟩ \\  & =t\,i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \lt t \lt 1.$ Along this segment, we have $x = t$ and $y = t.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t)) & =(2x-3y)\,i+(2y-5x)\,j \\  & =(2t-3t)\,i+(2t-5t)\,j \\  & =-t\,i-3t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the derivative, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

We can now compute the dot product:

$$
\begin{aligned}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t) & =(-t\,i-3t\,j)\cdot (i+j) \\  & =-t\cdot 1+(-3t)\cdot 1 \\  & =-4t\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the integral, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}r+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}r \\  & =-4+{\int }_{0}^{1}F({r}_{2}(t))\cdot {r}_{2}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4+{\int }_{0}^{1}(-4t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-4+[-2{t}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =-4+[-2+0] \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Line integrals of vector-valued functions share a fundamental connection with line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y.$

Consider a vector field $\mathbf F$ on $\mathbb R^2$ with components $P$ and $Q\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\mathbf F(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y)\,\mathbf j
$$

Now suppose that $C$ is a smooth curve on $\mathbb R^2,$ given by

$$
\mathbf r (t) = x(t)\,\mathbf i + y(t)\,\mathbf j, \qquad t\in [a,b].
$$

Then, we can write the line integral of $\mathbf F$ along $C$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following formula:

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y)  \,\textrm d y
$$

An analogous result holds for vector fields on $\mathbb R^3.$ That is, 

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\textrm d \mathbf r  = \int\limits_C P(x,y,z)\,\textrm d x + Q(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d y + R(x,y,z) \,\textrm d z
$$

where $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = P(x,y,z)\,\mathbf i + Q(x,y,z)\,\mathbf j + R(x,y,z)\,\mathbf k.$

Consider a vector field $\mathbf F$ on $\mathbb R^2$ with components $P$ and $Q\mathbin{:}$ 

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}F\cdot \text{d}r & ={\int }_{a}^{b}F(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\,i+Q(x(t),y(t))\,j)\cdot (\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}P(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+Q(x(t),y(t))\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{C}P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Reversing the Orientation of a Curve and Sums Over Unions of Paths
tutorials.problem:
Since there is a fundamental link between line integrals of vector-valued functions and line integrals with respect to $x$ and $y,$ it should be unsurprising that they share similar properties. We list two of them below:

- If $-C$ denotes the path obtained by reversing the orientation of $C,$ then

$$
\int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

- If $C = C_1\cup C_2$ is the union of two paths $C_1$ and $C_2$, then

$$
\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r 
= 
\int\limits_{C_1} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r + \int\limits_{C_2} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$

The first property has an intuitive meaning if we think about it in terms of the work done by a force on a particle. To see this, consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the line segment $\overline{AB},$ shown below. Let $C$ be the path defined by traversing the line segment from $A$ to $B.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/4f69f80d98d301410908f7ec867a89bdc834c22a51f224d9b00b80ceca39ab87.png)

 

Let $W(C)$ be the work done in moving the particle along $C.$ Since our particle moves in the same direction as the vector field, we have

$$
W(C) = \int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r > 0.
$$

However, if we move the particle from $B$ to $A,$ we expect the line integral to be negative. This is because the particle is now moving against $\mathbf F.$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14223647/assets/fe6b2e67d33a4993104406c88b1dc0dc897be33d034007ed581a75f741ddf620.png)

 

Therefore,

$$
W(-C) = \int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r < 0.
$$

We can show that the work done in moving the particle along $-C$ is the same as the work done in moving it along $C$ but with the opposite sign. That is

$$
W(-C) = -W(C).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\int\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r = -\int\limits_{C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathrm d \mathbf r.
$$
